title: Wood Thrush counts did not increase where acid wet deposition decreased most on 1,850 eastern US Breeding Bird Survey routes in 1987-2025
abstract: Hames et al. (2002) linked high acid wet deposition to a lower probability of Wood Thrush breeding in eastern North America. US sulfate deposition then decreased: at the eastern US Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) routes in this study, the median wet SO4 decreased from 19 to 5 kg/ha/yr between 1985-1994 and 2016-2025. We did a test of the prediction that Wood Thrush counts increase most where deposition decreased most. We used the BBS 2026 release (1966-2025, 2,496 routes east of 100 W) and NADP annual deposition grids (1985-2025). Poisson models had route-observer and Bird Conservation Region x year fixed effects and an observer first-year term. Wood Thrush counts changed by +10.7% per +10 kg/ha/yr of wet SO4 (95% CI +2.2% to +20.0%; within-region permutation p = 0.028). This sign is opposite to the prediction. The estimate was at the 77th percentile of 64 other forest species, so it does not show a species-specific effect. Results stayed positive or near zero in two periods, two region groups, with NO3 in place of SO4, and with segment detections as the response. With route-specific linear trends removed, the estimate was +2.2% (-4.7% to +9.7%), which permits a recovery of at most about 5% per 10 kg/ha/yr decrease. Route trends in 1966-1998 were more positive, not more negative, where deposition was high. The SO4 effect did not change with elevation. Veery, Hermit Thrush and Ovenbird showed no consistent recovery. Limitations: BBS counts measure relative abundance, not breeding attempts; exposure is interpolated wet deposition near the route start; soil calcium recovery can be slow; and regional changes that correlate with the deposition decrease can bias the estimates.
